video_title: Kavak's Playbook for Rebuilding a Company Around AI
gist: Ali Masa, head of AI at Latin American used-car marketplace Kavak, details how the company scrapped its multi-agent workflow architecture after Opus 4.5 shipped and rebuilt around one long-running agent per customer, each in its own virtual machine, instantiating 100,000-200,000 agents daily. He gives hard operating numbers - 96% of interactions and 95% of transactions agent-handled, agents converting 2.1x better than the human sales team, NPS tripled, car loans approved in under three minutes, warranties down ~20-26% - plus an AI-CEO experiment running a Mexican city's P&L that delivered 1.5x profit growth in its first month. His investment frame: spend as much on evals as on agents, tier your token spend by measurable ROI, and expect net-new AI-native companies rather than incumbents to capture the value.

insights.claim: Kavak designed its current architecture by asking what the company would look like if built in 2035 with GPT-10-level intelligence, then building that today rather than retrofitting AI onto the existing org.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: A reusable diligence question for any AI-transformation story: ask whether management designed backwards from future model capability or forwards from today's org chart.
insights.quote: The questions we ask ourselves is how would we build Kabak in 2035 with fable 10 or or or GPT 10 level intelligence and actually that company looks very different than than what we had built

insights.claim: Kavak spawns a dedicated long-running agent per customer with its own virtual machine, persistent memory of years of interactions, a CLI with access to every internal tool and API, and a long-term goal of maximizing that customer's lifetime value.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Per-customer agent instances with dedicated VMs imply a compute and orchestration bill that scales with customer count, not query count - a distinct infrastructure demand curve from chat-style deployments.
insights.quote: it's it's a virtual machine with an agent with access to memory and evals and the CLI where they can access every tool and every API in my company and the long-term goal

insights.claim: Kavak destroyed two years of working multi-agent graph and workflow infrastructure - the systems that had carried it to profitability and growth - after Opus 4.5 shipped, on the judgment that scaffolding now constrains rather than augments frontier model intelligence.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Signals that agent-orchestration tooling and graph frameworks face obsolescence risk with each model generation - a durability question for startups selling that layer.
insights.quote: But then Opus 4.5 came out and I realized like this isn't the right paradigm anymore. like the the intelligence now doesn't need like the graph and the multi- aent lattis work and harness because it will constraint this level of intelligence.

insights.claim: Masa advises builders to skip agentic workflows entirely and go straight to long-running agents with hard objectives, arguing that workflow-and-graph architectures are the wrong starting point rather than a necessary stepping stone.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Directly against the prevailing enterprise pattern of starting with narrow workflow automation; a fast-follower argument for greenfield teams.
insights.quote: like if I could advise everyone don't build agentic workflows to graphs or or functions or or objectives

insights.claim: Kavak's harness is explicitly designed to absorb recursive self-improvement and new frontier models released every month rather than to be re-engineered around each one.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Model-agnostic harness design is the hedge against the exact obsolescence event Kavak just lived through; look for it in AI-native company diligence.

insights.claim: Kavak instantiates between 100,000 and 200,000 agents per day, with individual agents running anywhere from three minutes to eight hours to three days before setting an alarm for their next task and sleeping.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: One of the few disclosed production agent-fleet counts; sets a real-world benchmark for compute demand per mid-size consumer business.
insights.quote: Every day between a 100 and 200,000 agents get instantiated in a day. They wake up, they work sometimes for three minutes, sometimes for eight hours, sometimes for three days, and they like set an alarm clock for their next task and they go back to sleep.

insights.claim: Agents handle 96% of all customer interactions and 95% of all transactions at Kavak, with humans remaining only at physical car handover.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Demonstrates end-to-end agent handling of high-ticket regulated commerce is already in production, not pilot - raises the bar for what 'AI adoption' should mean in comps.
insights.quote: So so to give you a sense of the scale 90 like 96% of all interactions uh are handled by agents. So so no humans there. Um like 95% of all transactions are completely handled by by agents.

insights.claim: Masa says he is now investing more in tokens than in knowledge workers, treating inference spend as a direct substitute for headcount budget.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: A concrete instance of opex shifting from payroll to compute - the substitution that underwrites inference-demand and labor-displacement theses.
insights.quote: I'm investing more today in tokens than in knowledge workers.

insights.claim: Masa grades token spend in three tiers: tier three tokens go to production agents with directly measurable per-token ROI, tier two are dev-tool tokens measurable only indirectly, and tier one is ungoverned employee use of chat and coding tools with no visibility into value.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: A practical screen for whether an enterprise's rising AI spend is compounding or burning - ask which tier the incremental dollars sit in.
insights.quote: level tier three tokens the most valuable are this agents where you can get the ROI of each specific token and I can do that now. That's great news for me because I'm growing and because I know the ROI of each token

insights.claim: Masa warns that companies spending hundreds of millions of dollars on tokens after achieving adoption are mistaking spend for transformation, because most of that spend sits in the tier with no measurable return.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Implies a coming wave of enterprise AI budget scrutiny; adoption metrics in vendor disclosures may not convert to renewals.
insights.quote: So I see a lot of companies spending now huge amounts and they say okay I got adoption I'm just spending like hundreds of millions of dollars in in tokens now

insights.claim: Kavak's agent fleet shares learning across instances, so a mistake made by one agent is absorbed by all 200,000 agents the next day - a feedback loop Masa credits for growth, results and customer satisfaction.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Fleet-wide learning is the structural advantage agents hold over human teams; it compounds with customer volume and is hard for a late adopter to replicate.
insights.quote: if they make a mistake, they learn it and the next day, not just them, but the other 200,000 agents will have learned from that mistake

insights.claim: Kavak spends roughly the same engineer time, tokens and money building evals as building the agents themselves, treating eval quality as the brake that determines maximum safe deployment speed.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: A 1:1 eval-to-agent spend ratio is a concrete diligence benchmark and a sizable, underappreciated line item in agent TCO.
insights.quote: we spend about the same amount of time, engineer time, tokens, and and and money on building the evils than building the agents

insights.claim: Masa inverts the usual risk posture: rather than going slow because evals are weak, he asks how fast the company can go given eval quality, arguing companies that move slowly do so because they lack brakes, not because caution is correct.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Reframes AI governance spend as a speed enabler rather than a compliance cost - the argument enterprise eval vendors need to win budget.
insights.quote: I like to move extremely fast, but in order to move fast, you need to have brakes, right? Imagine a car. Uh you'll hit on the gas just if you have the right brakes.

insights.claim: Kavak evaluates agents on business outcomes - did the customer convert, get the loan approved, re-engage later - and Masa says companies measuring call counts or call minutes are tracking superficial KPIs that break precisely where it matters.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Outcome-linked evals are the tell separating real agent deployments from demo-grade ones when assessing AI-services and agent vendors.
insights.quote: Like the important thing is did this customer convert? Is it bringing value to the customer and is the customer happy to re-engage with us after a while?

themes.theme: Agents selling and underwriting high-ticket regulated products

insights.claim: Kavak never built customer support agents - it built sales agents first, deliberately pointing AI at the highest-leverage revenue task rather than the lowest-risk one.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Cuts against the market's assumption that customer service is the entry wedge for enterprise AI; sales-agent budgets may be the larger pool.
insights.quote: So so we never built customer support or customer service agents. We we built like sales agents.

insights.claim: Kavak's sales agent converts 2.1x better than its human sales team, up from 50% better at launch, while tripling NPS and customer satisfaction scores.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: A rare disclosed head-to-head on agent versus human sales productivity, and the improving trend line matters more than the level.
insights.quote: We tripled uh NPS and customer satisfaction score by putting the the agent in front of the of the customer. And it at first it converted like 50% more than our human team and now it's converting over that like 2.1 uh x more.

insights.claim: Kavak collapsed a sales process that previously required 15 different experts across 15 teams - car advisory, financing, insurance, trade-in quoting across 20,000 SKUs - into a single 'mega expert' agent that beats the human specialist in each function.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Bundling specialist roles into one agent is where the org-cost savings concentrate; look for the same collapse in insurance, mortgage and wealth distribution.

insights.claim: Kavak approves car loans in under three minutes in markets where the norm is two months or more, and its vertical integration lets a struggling borrower return the car and swap into a cheaper one with lower payments rather than default.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Vertical integration plus agent underwriting is a credible loss-mitigation mechanism in thin-file emerging-market consumer credit - relevant to LatAm fintech credit models.
insights.quote: usually in in Mexico and and in some emerging markets it'll get like two months or or or or more to get a car loan approved. Um, we usually approve it in under three minutes.

insights.claim: Because car and large personal loan decisions take customers three to four months, Kavak's agents optimize for knowing the customer over that window and converting when they are ready, with deep personalization of interest rate, risk assessment and maximum loan amount.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Long-cycle high-ticket categories are where per-customer persistent agents earn their compute cost - a screen for which verticals the architecture transfers to.

insights.claim: Kavak reframed itself from a transactional business measuring cars bought and sold to a relational one where agents are assigned to most of its 10 million database customers, and Masa estimates activating just 1% of that base is worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the dormant-base monetization thesis: agents make previously uneconomic long-tail customer relationships worth working.
insights.quote: now I have 10 million customers in my database and I have agents assigned to most of them with the task of maximizing their lifetime value. Now, we're selling cars and and and personal loans and very high ticket items. So just activating 1% of this customer base, it's like hundreds of millions of of dollars

themes.theme: Org redesign: Jedi Academy, flat teams, and an AI CEO

insights.claim: Kavak carved out one Mexican city as an AI CEO experiment, putting an agent in a harness with authority over that city's P&L; it missed its first-month goal of doubling profits but delivered 1.5x, roughly 50% more profit, while improving customer satisfaction, inventory rotation and financing penetration.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: The clearest datapoint yet that agentic management, not just agentic labor, produces P&L movement - and it had only been running six weeks.
insights.quote: The goal of the first month was to double the the the profits of of Guavaka. It didn't reach it but it was 1.5x like 50% more profits.

insights.claim: The AI CEO works by exhaustive micromanagement - reviewing every number and customer, forecasting, then messaging physical workers with daily plans and collecting voice notes back on progress - which Masa argues is why it outperformed rather than any strategic brilliance.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: The mechanism is attention capacity, not judgment - meaning the advantage transfers to any operationally complex, data-rich management role.
insights.quote: going into every single number every single customer making the perfect forecast and going to micromanage every single things that needs to be executed every day to reach a plan

insights.claim: Kavak runs an internal six-week training program called the Jedi Academy that Masa designed and leads himself, taking everyone from the CEO to mechanics to AI engineers through to shipping state-of-the-art agents to production, and it is continuously rewritten because external programs cannot keep pace.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: In-house, continuously refreshed AI training is emerging as a required capability - and a headwind for traditional executive-education and enterprise-training providers.
insights.quote: we train everyone and after six weeks they launch state-of-the-art uh agents AI agents to production and it's mechanics and and finance guys and engineers is like everyone can do it

insights.claim: Kavak gave employees an explicit binary - retrain for the agentic company or leave - and Masa says the result strengthened rather than damaged culture.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Counters the assumption that forced AI transitions destroy morale; relevant to how aggressively management teams can move.
insights.quote: You have the choice to like train and and get the skills to perform in this new reality, in this new world. Um, or maybe leave Kavak if this is not for you, but this is the way we're going.

insights.claim: Kavak's org is now flat, senior, cross-functional teams that either build agents, work for agents, or operate in the physical world in front of customers - with agents sometimes acting as the boss of humans.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: A concrete template for the post-middle-management org; the three-way role taxonomy is a usable lens for assessing headcount plans.
insights.quote: any process it's really a collaboration of agents and humans and sometimes like agents are the bosses or of of humans and sometimes humans are designing the agents

insights.claim: Kavak inverted the human-in-the-loop pattern: instead of escalating stuck cases to a tier-2 queue where the loop is never closed and no training data is generated, its agents call an API to request help and a human answers, keeping the agent as case owner.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Escalation design determines whether a deployment compounds or plateaus - a specific technical detail to probe in any agent-vendor diligence.
insights.quote: if an agent hits a wall or cancels something, it'll call this API saying I need help. And on the other side, it's not an agent or software, it's a human helping them out. But if you map this out in an org chart, it's really human teams that have an agent.

insights.claim: Kavak still hires and trains humans for physical-world roles, retaining around 800 mechanics in Mexico, and instead ships them an AI sidekick called El Mike built on the same harness that guides inspections - cutting warranty claims by roughly 20-26% while speeding inspection and repair.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Marks the current capability boundary - dexterity and physical senses - and quantifies augmentation value where substitution is not yet possible.
insights.quote: warranties came down around like 20 26% since we since we launched and customer satisfaction again went up

themes.theme: Creative destruction and the incumbent adoption gap

insights.claim: Masa argues AI transformation must be top-down with leadership holding a specific three-to-five-year picture of the company, and that hackathon-and-use-case sponsorship programs - the dominant enterprise approach - simply do not work.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: If bottom-up adoption programs are structurally ineffective, enterprise AI revenue concentrates in vendors selling to CEOs, not to innovation teams.
insights.quote: It's like be very clear on what the company will look like in three or five years and then start building that and be like very vertical in in guiding your troops towards that.

insights.claim: Masa invokes Schumpeterian creative destruction to argue value from AI will accrue to net-new companies destroying incumbents, not to incumbents adopting AI, because no CEO of a large public company will credibly bet on demolishing forty years of built assets.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: A direct argument for venture exposure to AI-native challengers over incumbent AI-adoption stories in disrupted verticals.
insights.quote: it's really hard for a CEO today, especially of a large company or public company, to go and say, "Hey, like I'm betting everything on AI. Uh the company has to look this way. I'll like destroy and rebuild everything I've been building for the past 40 years to become an AI native company."

insights.claim: Masa uses the electrification lag as the base rate: Edison's efficient dynamo and the enabling technologies existed by 1879-1881, yet factories that merely swapped a coal engine for an electric one got about 6% efficiency, while redesigning around distributed small dynamos on a flat greenfield site delivered roughly 3x productivity - a forty-year gap before Ford.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Sets the expected shape of AI productivity diffusion: a long lag, then step-change gains concentrated in redesigned firms - implying near-term aggregate productivity data will disappoint.
insights.quote: you could have built Ford's factory 40 years before Ford. The technology was there, everything was there.

insights.claim: Masa predicts superficial AI adoption delivers 6-10% improvement rather than 10x, framing the gap as the innovator's dilemma at industrial scale.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: A quantified expectation to test against reported AI ROI in incumbent earnings calls - single-digit gains confirm the thesis rather than refute it.
insights.quote: in the end, that'll give you a 6% or a 10% improvement, not a 10x improvement. And it's like the innovator's dilemma at an industrial uh scale.

insights.claim: Masa argues the right target for recursive self-improvement is the organization rather than the model, because economic value over 4,000 years has been delivered by organizations, not individuals - so the compounding loop to build is a self-improving company that continuously absorbs newer models.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: Shifts the RSI debate from lab capability to firm-level architecture - the exponential to underwrite is in company value creation, not model IQ.
insights.quote: economic value in humanity for for the past 4,000 years has been delivered by organization, not not by individuals. So what you want to self-improve and to engage in that loop is the organization that can deliver more economic value.

insights.claim: Masa tells founders to design against a merely linear extrapolation of AI improvement rather than an exponential one, arguing that even the conservative trend line is enough to justify building for a radically different future.
insights.speaker: Ali Masa (head of AI, Kavak)
insights.so_what: A deliberately conservative planning assumption that still implies aggressive product bets - useful for stress-testing AI-native business plans.
insights.quote: It's just a uh it's not even an exponential. Just just map a trend that's linear. If things keeps getting like AI keeps getting better at a linear scale and just build for that
